questions.question: What does Fastify do, and who calls or runs it?
questions.answer: Fastify is a low-overhead Node.js web framework. Application developers instantiate its exported factory, register routes and call listen; HTTP clients then trigger those handlers. It is a framework dependency rather than a single fixed application server shipped for one business domain.

questions.question: Name the principal Fastify components and their responsibilities.
questions.answer: fastify.js constructs the public instance and wires internal modules; lib/server.js constructs server/listen machinery; lib/route.js registers and dispatches routes; lib/handle-request.js coordinates parsing/validation/hooks and handler invocation; lib/wrap-thenable.js settles asynchronous handler results into replies. These are modules within one package, not independent npm packages.

questions.question: Which languages, runtime/build tools and package boundaries organize Fastify?
questions.answer: The root fastify npm package uses CommonJS JavaScript on Node.js, with fastify.js as main and fastify.d.ts TypeScript declarations. package.json scripts run borp unit tests, tstyche type checks, ESLint and generated validation/error-serializer builds. lib modules belong to the same package; require dependencies are not automatically workspace packages.
requiredFacts: One root npm package with fastify.js main

questions.question: Where does public-library use to create a Fastify server begin?
questions.answer: package.json main resolves fastify.js. Its function fastify(serverOptions) is exported as module.exports, and also as .fastify and .default. A consumer calls the factory before get/listen; this exported factory is the selected public entry rather than an unconditional executable startup.

questions.question: Where is X = sending the resolved value returned by an async route handler implemented?
questions.answer: lib/handle-request.js preHandlerCallbackInner calls context.handler and detects a non-null result with a then function, passing it to wrapThenable. lib/wrap-thenable.js attaches fulfillment/rejection handlers; fulfillment sends the payload subject to hijack/sent/connection guards, while rejection marks reply as error and sends it unless already sent. It does not treat every return value as a promise.

questions.question: Which internal modules does A = lib/handle-request.js directly use, and what proves each direction?
questions.answer: Its explicit relative requires point to wrap-thenable, validation, hooks, errors, error-status, symbols and content-type. validation.validate is locally named validateSchema; hooks exports preValidationHookRunner and preHandlerHookRunner. node:diagnostics_channel is external Node runtime API, not an internal module. These imports prove handle-request -> dependency, not reverse calls.
requiredFacts: Node diagnostics is external; direction follows require

questions.question: For R = a bodyless request reaching handleRequest whose configured handler returns a fulfilled promise, trace the path to reply.send and identify dynamic boundaries.
questions.answer: handleRequest calls handler for a bodyless method; handler enters preValidationCallback directly or via hooks; validationCompleted enters preHandlerCallback directly or via preHandler hooks; preHandlerCallbackInner invokes context.handler. A thenable result goes to wrapThenable, whose fulfillment branch sends the payload if guards allow. Hook functions, validators, configured context.handler and promise settlement are runtime boundaries. Validation/errors or an already sent reply can stop this path; the supplied assumptions do not identify a particular application handler.
requiredFacts: Hooks/validation/application callback and promise are dynamic; early exits exist

questions.question: If Y = lib/handle-request.js exports change, which production modules directly consume them?
questions.answer: lib/route.js requires the default handleRequest and invokes it from runPreParsing (or supplies a bound callback to preParsing hooks). lib/reply.js requires the Symbol.for(internals) export and uses preHandlerCallback in its notFound path. These direct dependencies support reviewing route lifecycle and not-found behavior; they do not prove all routes or plugins fail after any change.

questions.question: Which test exercises X through public server use, and how does it enter?
questions.answer: test/async-await.test.js async await test creates Fastify, registers an async GET handler returning {hello:world}, listens on an ephemeral port and fetches it. It asserts status 200 and the JSON body. This enters through real HTTP route dispatch in the test source, unlike a direct call of wrapThenable; no claim is made that the test was run in this oracle preparation.
requiredFacts: fetch response checked for 200 and expected JSON
Source inspection is not execution evidence

questions.question: Where does Z = a QUERY request lacking Content-Type enter and get handled?
questions.answer: handleRequest reads request.method and headers for body-carrying supported methods. In the QUERY branch, missing content-type marks kReplyIsError, sends status 400 with FST_ERR_ROUTE_MISSING_CONTENT_TYPE(method), and returns before content parsing or the application handler. This differs from a nonempty body with invalid media type, which has a later 415 branch.
requiredFacts: QUERY missing content-type enters explicit check
Sets error marker and sends 400 FST_ERR_ROUTE_MISSING_CONTENT_TYPE
Returns before parser/handler; later 415 is distinct
